seed_title: Evaluation of the Canadian Forces Military Police Academy
source_title: Evaluation of the Canadian Forces Military Police Academy
evaluating_organisation: Department of National Defence, Assistant Deputy Minister (Review Services)
evaluation_question: How well does the Academy deliver efficient, effective and inclusive military-police training, modernise its courses and respond to external reviews?
methods: Graduate and instructor surveys, stakeholder interviews, course and end-course review analysis, training and financial data, and comparisons with other policing academies.
findings: Training remained broadly effective and cost-efficient, but instructor shortages and underused specialists weakened delivery. Bilingual provision, diversity, digital learning and victim-centred training had gaps, while feedback rarely supported systematic improvement.
recommendations: Expand the qualified instructor pool; complete external-review actions, especially trauma-informed victim-rights training; and establish formal internal and external feedback mechanisms.
recommendation_basis: Formal recommendations, summarised
conclusions: The Academy fulfils a critical role, but stronger teaching capacity, victim-support training and performance feedback are needed to protect training quality and readiness.
note: Methods summarised from evidence described throughout the report; no standalone methods annex.
transferable_lesson: Use formal feedback from learners, instructors and external stakeholders to guide continuing improvements to training.
transferable_lesson_rationale: Recommendation 3 explicitly calls for internal and external feedback mechanisms to support training improvements.

seed_title: Evaluation of Canadian Coast Guard Marine Navigation
source_title: Evaluation of Canadian Coast Guard Marine Navigation
evaluating_organisation: Fisheries and Oceans Canada and Canadian Coast Guard, Evaluation Division
notes: Evaluation conducted by Fisheries and Oceans Canada and the Canadian Coast Guard, then published by National Defence after the September 2025 transfer. Report dated December 2025; catalogue identifier is D2-721/2026E-PDF.
evaluation_question: What value do marine-navigation services provide, what resources support them, are intended outcomes achieved, and how prepared are the programmes for digitalisation?
methods: Triangulated document review, 44 interviews, three site visits, performance and financial analysis, and a case study of digital navigation standards.
findings: Services supplied timely safety information, but aids-to-navigation and icebreaking targets were not fully met. Limited vessels, ageing equipment, weak indicators and fragmented guidance constrained delivery and digital modernisation.
recommendations: Develop national Indigenous-reconciliation guidance and a digital change-management strategy; review the aids-to-navigation programme; and improve performance measures for navigation aids and marine communications.
recommendation_basis: Formal recommendations, summarised
conclusions: Services are essential to safety, sovereignty and economic activity. Clearer governance, coordination and performance measurement are needed for sustainable modernisation.
note: Industry participation was limited; the evaluators did not generalise from the small industry sample.
transferable_lesson: Support digital modernisation with a change-management strategy that clarifies responsibilities, communication and collaboration.
transferable_lesson_rationale: Recommendation 2 explicitly specifies these elements for modernising marine-navigation services.

seed_title: Evaluation of Land Equipment Acquisition Program
source_title: Evaluation of Land Equipment Acquisition Program
evaluating_organisation: Department of National Defence, Assistant Deputy Minister (Review Services)
evaluation_question: Do land acquisitions use agile procurement, keep pace with technology, close capability gaps, benefit from effective costing and measure operational outcomes?
methods: Two acquisition case studies, document and financial review, 21 interviews, two surveys, three site visits and focus groups, with evidence triangulation.
findings: Machine-gun upgrades met military needs; patrol vehicles met original requirements but struggled with evolving needs. Both projects were broadly on budget but late. Agile procurement, user consultation and operational performance data were weak.
recommendations: Formalise consultation with users, stakeholders and external experts; strengthen tactical and capability performance measurement. Also implement existing recommendations on agile procurement and gender-based analysis throughout acquisition.
recommendation_basis: Formal recommendations and linked prior recommendations, summarised
conclusions: More adaptable procurement, consultation and outcome measurement are needed to ensure equipment continues to meet changing operational requirements.
note: Findings centre on patrol vehicles and machine-gun upgrades, rather than every land acquisition.
transferable_lesson: Meeting an original equipment specification is insufficient if the acquisition cannot adapt to evolving operational needs.
transferable_lesson_rationale: Generalises from the patrol vehicle meeting original requirements while struggling with evolving capability needs; it is not stated as a universal rule.

seed_title: Evaluation of Ready Joint and Combined Forces
source_title: Report Summary: Evaluation of Ready Joint and Combined Forces
evaluating_organisation: Department of National Defence, Assistant Deputy Minister (Review Services)
notes: Official source is a five-page report summary including a management action plan. A separate full report was not located. Seed author is blank; publisher verified from the official source.
evaluation_question: How effectively does the programme prepare integrated and interoperable joint and combined forces through training and readiness coordination?
methods: Document and administrative-data review, survey, questionnaire, key-informant interviews and site visits covering fiscal years 2017/18–2021/22.
findings: Personnel and training shortages, inadequate classified communications and inaccurate readiness reporting constrained interoperability. No organisation coordinated joint readiness comprehensively, and exercise priorities were unclear.
recommendations: Establish a mechanism to coordinate and prioritise joint and combined initiatives, supported by updated readiness guidance and departmental strategic direction.
recommendation_basis: Formal recommendation and management actions, summarised
conclusions: The programme was not fully meeting responsibilities or performance targets. Planned changes to readiness priorities and joint training could improve delivery.
note: Based on the published five-page report summary, not a full evaluation report.
transferable_lesson: Establish a mechanism to coordinate and prioritise initiatives that depend on contributions from multiple military organisations.
transferable_lesson_rationale: The report's single recommendation explicitly requires coordination and prioritisation of joint and combined initiatives.

seed_title: Evaluation of Canadian Armed Forces Retention
source_title: Evaluation of Canadian Armed Forces Retention
evaluating_organisation: Department of National Defence, Assistant Deputy Minister (Review Services)
evaluation_question: Where and why does voluntary attrition occur, do retention efforts reflect needs and best practice, and are those efforts coordinated and positioned to improve retention?
methods: Workforce and attrition data, stakeholder interviews, research and international comparisons, plus case studies of the Naval Experience Program and pilot-pay restructuring.
findings: Early departures reflected training delays and difficulty adapting. Relocation and institutional dissatisfaction affected mid-career staff; pension eligibility drove later exits. Local initiatives were promising, but strategic coordination and awareness were weak.
recommendations: Explore a forces-wide experience programme; share successful local retention practices; brief leaders on Transition Group services; and formalise evidence-based consultation on compensation changes.
recommendation_basis: Formal recommendations, summarised
conclusions: Retention needs responses tailored to career stage and better coordination of local initiatives, support services and compensation decisions.
conclusion_basis: Synthesis of findings; no standalone conclusion
note: Limited to Regular Force voluntary releases. Methods are described through the evidence used, without a standalone methods annex.
transferable_lesson: Capture and share successful local retention practices centrally so other commands can learn from and replicate them.
transferable_lesson_rationale: Recommendation 2 and its management action explicitly propose a central repository to share and replicate successful local practices.

seed_title: Evaluation of the Canadian Armed Forces Strategy to Achieve Fundamental Change for the Reserve Force
source_title: Evaluation of the Canadian Armed Forces Strategy to Achieve Fundamental Change for the Reserve Force
evaluating_organisation: Department of National Defence, Assistant Deputy Minister (Review Services)
notes: The report describes a developmental evaluation approach. The seed Process Evaluation label is retained separately.
evaluation_question: Is the Reserve Force’s New Vision relevant to military objectives, and what could prevent its implementation and integration into force readiness?
methods: Developmental evaluation of the emerging strategy, using stakeholder feedback, command-team survey evidence, personnel data, policy analysis and UK/Australian comparisons.
findings: Reservists were not integrated into readiness planning. Fragmented policies, inadequate data, resource constraints and distinct recruitment/retention challenges limited progress; stakeholders differed over assigning unique reserve capabilities.
recommendations: No formal recommendations. The conclusion calls for agreement on reserve roles, integrated readiness planning, coherent policy and data, and sustained monitoring of recruitment and retention objectives.
recommendation_basis: No formal recommendations; priorities stated in conclusion
conclusions: The New Vision addresses relevant problems, but fundamental change requires a shared purpose and a sustained, coordinated implementation effort.
note: Developmental evaluation undertaken while the strategy was being drafted; it does not establish realised long-term impacts.
transferable_lesson: Agree a shared organisational purpose before translating a reform vision into workforce targets, policies and readiness plans.
transferable_lesson_rationale: Extends the conclusion about agreement on Reserve Force roles into a broader sequencing principle for organisational reform.

seed_title: Evaluation of the IDEaS Program
source_title: Evaluation of the IDEaS Program
evaluating_organisation: Department of National Defence, Assistant Deputy Minister (Review Services)
evaluation_question: Does IDEaS remain relevant, engage innovators and networks, produce useful defence solutions, and deliver its activities cost-effectively?
methods: Document and programme/financial-data review, 15 interviews, two stakeholder surveys and benchmarking against eight countries’ innovation programmes.
findings: IDEaS engaged smaller firms and universities and advanced useful solutions. Strategic direction, stakeholder engagement, transition towards commercialisation and use of grants/contributions funding needed improvement.
recommendations: Strengthen strategic direction and governance, particularly challenge selection; sustain engagement across programme stages; and explore greater use of transfer-payment funding.
recommendation_basis: Formal recommendations, summarised
conclusions: The programme remains relevant and supports Canadian defence innovation, but clearer priorities, stronger partnerships and improved funding use would increase its contribution.
note: The departmental procurement process was outside the evaluation’s scope.
transferable_lesson: Design innovation programmes around the transition from promising solutions to adoption, alongside attracting innovators and funding development.
transferable_lesson_rationale: Draws a broader programme-design lesson from concerns about next steps and commercialisation; the report does not explicitly prescribe this design principle.

seed_title: Evaluation of the Military Training and Cooperation Program
source_title: Evaluation of the Military Training and Cooperation Program
evaluating_organisation: Department of National Defence, Assistant Deputy Minister (Review Services)
notes: Seed publication date is blank. February 2024 edition selected as the latest matching evaluation found; May 2019 edition also exists at the alternative link. Edition choice requires confirmation. Published report contains redactions under Access to Information Act section 15(1).
evaluation_question: Is military training cooperation aligned with government priorities, effective in building partner capability and defence relationships, and governed and resourced efficiently?
methods: 29 interviews, three surveys with 271 responses, four country/course case studies, document review and comparison with Australian, US and New Zealand programmes.
findings: Training improved participants’ skills and supported defence diplomacy, but strategic priorities and outcome data were weak. Administrative costs were high, pandemic underspending was substantial, and coordination with other departments and allies was limited.
recommendations: Strengthen governance and strategic direction; collect evidence connecting training to programme objectives; and coordinate planning and information-sharing with other departments and allied programmes.
recommendation_basis: Formal recommendations, summarised
conclusions: The programme remains relevant and contributes positively to defence relationships, but clearer priorities and stronger evidence are needed as its responsibilities expand.
note: Uses the February 2024 edition. The seed has no date and a May 2019 edition also exists; the published report contains redactions.
transferable_lesson: Distinguish improvements in trainees' skills from improvements in their organisation's capability, and collect evidence for both.
transferable_lesson_rationale: Generalises from improved individual abilities alongside insufficient evidence of partner-country military capacity; the report recommends stronger outcome data.

seed_title: Evaluation of Using Data as a Strategic Asset in the Department of National Defence / Canadian Armed Forces
source_title: Evaluation of Using Data as a Strategic Asset in the Department of National Defence/Canadian Armed Forces
evaluating_organisation: Department of National Defence, Assistant Deputy Minister (Review Services)
evaluation_question: How far has Defence used data to support decisions, and are governance, integrated data management, lifecycle controls and policy alignment sufficient?
methods: Qualitative document review, interviews involving 49 people, and case studies of 14 decision-support systems across nine defence organisations, with triangulation.
findings: Foundational tools and organisations had developed, but systems formed an uncoordinated patchwork. Enterprise and military priorities were unclear, governance was fragmented, and data was not managed consistently as an organisational asset.
recommendations: Set defence-wide and military-specific priorities for decision-support systems; establish governance to communicate priorities, monitor delivery and report progress.
recommendation_basis: Formal recommendations, summarised
conclusions: Defence was not obtaining full value from its decision-support investments. Shared priorities and clear accountability are needed to turn local progress into organisation-wide capability.
note: An organisation-wide overview, not an in-depth assessment of each system or a formal review of separate IT and information-management functions.
transferable_lesson: Set organisation-wide priorities for decision-support systems and give governance responsibility for communicating priorities, monitoring delivery and reporting progress.
transferable_lesson_rationale: The recommendations explicitly require shared system-development priorities and governance that communicates, monitors and reports against them.

seed_title: Carrier Strike - Preparing for Deployment
source_title: Carrier Strike – Preparing for deployment
notes: Seed Impact Evaluation label is retained; publisher categorises this as a value-for-money report.
evaluation_question: Has the Ministry of Defence managed Carrier Strike effectively since 2017, and is it positioned to deliver and sustain the full capability?
methods: Interviews, programme and financial-data review, assessment of cost models, visits to Portsmouth and RAF Marham, and observation of programme governance.
findings: Two carriers, 18 jets and much supporting infrastructure had been delivered. Radar and resupply capabilities lagged, while future development, operating and support costs remained unclear.
recommendations: Clarify capability ambitions and milestones; establish comprehensive operating costs and a funded enhancement plan; strengthen cross-command accountability; and apply lessons from exercises.
recommendation_basis: Formal recommendations, summarised
conclusions: Major assets were delivered, but achieving value for money depended on completing supporting capabilities and aligning ambitions, funding and responsibilities.
note: Assesses the position in 2020; does not evaluate military utility or operational deployment plans.
transferable_lesson: Treat delivery of major platforms as one part of capability delivery: fund and coordinate the support systems needed to use them.
transferable_lesson_rationale: Generalises from delivered carriers and aircraft whose radar, resupply and future support arrangements remained incomplete.

seed_title: The Afghanistan Response Route
source_title: The Afghanistan Response Route
notes: Factual report: explicitly does not evaluate management of or spending on the scheme. The NAO website category is Report - Value for money; this is not a statement about the evaluation design.
evaluation_question: What decisions established the Afghanistan Response Route, how many people were being resettled, and what costs had been incurred or forecast?
methods: Review of MoD financial and management information and Cabinet committee papers, with discussions involving MoD, Cabinet Office and Treasury officials.
findings: Following the data breach, 3,383 people had arrived through the route by June 2025. MoD estimated £400 million spent and £450 million still to spend, but did not separately account for scheme costs or sufficiently substantiate these estimates.
recommendations: None issued; the report establishes facts for parliamentary scrutiny.
recommendation_basis: No formal recommendations
conclusions: No evaluative conclusion was issued. The report establishes the resettlement position while highlighting uncertainty over the completeness and accuracy of cost estimates.
conclusion_basis: Synthesis of factual findings; no evaluative conclusion
note: Financial information was reviewed, not audited. The investigation does not assess scheme management or value for money.
transferable_lesson: For sensitive programmes, design accounting records that preserve traceable programme costs while respecting confidentiality requirements.
transferable_lesson_rationale: Inferred from costs being combined with wider resettlement spending and estimates lacking assurance; the report issues no accounting-design recommendation.

seed_title: Defence Inventory Management
source_title: Defence inventory management
evaluation_question: Has MoD addressed longstanding inventory weaknesses and established arrangements to deliver efficient, resilient inventory management and value for money?
methods: Interviews with MoD, military commands, procurement teams and Leidos; document and financial-data analysis; and visits to seven logistics and storage sites.
findings: Logistics and commodity procurement improved, but fragmented processes, ageing IT and poor data persisted. Stock imbalances and staff shortages constrained readiness and threatened transformation programmes.
recommendations: Define required inventory levels; improve commodity planning and consumption data; coordinate surplus disposal; assess workforce skills; and prioritise resources for inventory transformation.
recommendation_basis: Formal recommendations, summarised
conclusions: Despite improvements, MoD was not yet organised to achieve value for money. Sustained investment and organisational change were needed to reduce waste and improve resilience.
note: Summarises the position at the September 2023 report date.
transferable_lesson: Treat inventory reform as organisational change requiring skilled staff, consistent processes and reliable data, alongside investment in IT.
transferable_lesson_rationale: Synthesises the report's account of transformation dependencies and staffing gaps into a broader implementation lesson.

seed_title: Government Cyber Resilience
source_title: Government cyber resilience
evaluation_question: Are government efforts to improve cyber resilience keeping pace with the threat and on course to meet its strategic objectives?
methods: 42 interviews, thematic analysis, and review of strategy documents, GovAssure assessments, threat information, legacy-system data and workforce evidence.
findings: Cyber resilience was weaker than previously estimated. Critical control gaps, vulnerable legacy systems and skills shortages persisted. Progress was too slow to achieve the 2025 critical-functions target; the 2030 ambition remained challenging.
recommendations: Create a resourced implementation plan with clear accountability; strengthen central coordination and assurance; prioritise legacy-system risks; improve incident preparedness; and address cyber workforce gaps.
recommendation_basis: Formal recommendations, summarised
conclusions: Government needed urgent action on skills, accountability and legacy IT to catch up with the severe cyber threat and protect public services.
note: Findings and target assessments reflect the January 2025 publication, not a later assessment of target achievement.
transferable_lesson: Address cyber skills shortages, accountability for risk and vulnerable legacy IT to improve resilience against serious cyber threats.
transferable_lesson_rationale: The conclusion explicitly identifies these three conditions as necessary for government to catch up with the cyber threat.

seed_title: Improving Single Living Accommodation
source_title: Improving Single Living Accommodation
evaluation_question: Does MoD provide single living accommodation that meets service needs cost-effectively, and is it positioned to improve future provision?
methods: Interviews, service-personnel discussion groups, accommodation and survey-data analysis, document review and international comparisons; evidence was triangulated against asset-management practice.
findings: Accommodation condition and satisfaction had declined. Reactive maintenance, weak cost and occupancy information, unclear standards and fragmented planning undermined provision; future investment lacked a clear understanding of demand.
recommendations: Appoint a senior sponsor; improve estate data and booking systems; define acceptable standards using residents’ experience; review charges; and coordinate investment with wider accommodation plans.
recommendation_basis: Formal recommendations, summarised
conclusions: MoD was not meeting its accommodation commitment and could not demonstrate value for money. Better governance, information and sustained investment were required.
note: Cost and bed-space data contained significant gaps and inconsistencies; pandemic restrictions limited some fieldwork.
transferable_lesson: Define acceptable accommodation standards using both building condition and residents' experience, then regularly report progress against those standards.
transferable_lesson_rationale: Recommendation 20(e) explicitly links standards and progress reporting to building condition and the lived experience of residents.

seed_title: Improving the performance of major equipment contracts
source_title: Improving the performance of major equipment contracts
evaluation_question: Why do major defence-equipment contracts underperform, and what changes could improve their delivery and value for money?
methods: Detailed examination of 20 major programmes, interviews with departmental teams and suppliers, programme-data and document review, and commissioned RAND research on persistent acquisition problems.
findings: Delays and cost growth reflected supplier underperformance, weak contract management, underestimated technical complexity and short-term affordability decisions. Staff turnover, skills shortages and inconsistent learning compounded these problems.
recommendations: Demonstrate lessons learned in business cases; sustain commercial reforms; address skills and staff continuity; use supplier performance in procurement decisions; and reassess value for money when programmes change materially.
recommendation_basis: Formal recommendations, summarised
conclusions: MoD had not optimised value for money from its largest contracts. Lasting improvement required sustained leadership, resources and routine learning across programmes.
note: The 20 programmes were selected purposefully; findings are not a statistical assessment of the entire equipment portfolio.
transferable_lesson: Require new programme business cases to demonstrate how lessons from comparable programmes and past supplier relationships have been applied.
transferable_lesson_rationale: Recommendation 23(a) explicitly requires programme teams to demonstrate this learning in initial business cases.

seed_title: Investigation into military support for Ukraine
source_title: Investigation into military support for Ukraine
notes: Investigation explicitly does not evaluate value for money or effectiveness of the equipment and training provided. Seed Value for Money Evaluation label is retained separately.
evaluation_question: What military equipment, training and funding has the UK provided to Ukraine, how is support managed, and what are the implications for UK capability?
methods: 18 interviews, financial and programme-document review, and visits to training facilities, equipment warehouses and a lessons-review conference.
findings: The UK committed £7.8 billion for support through March 2025 and trained at least 42,050 personnel. Rapid initial arrangements became more structured, but replacing donated stocks and balancing training capacity created demands on UK readiness.
recommendations: No formal recommendations. The concluding remarks call for continued balancing of Ukraine’s needs, UK strategic interests and the UK’s own equipment stocks and training provision.
recommendation_basis: No formal recommendations; priority in concluding remarks
conclusions: MoD delivered substantial, internationally coordinated support and improved oversight. Future support needed to be balanced with maintaining the UK’s military capabilities.
note: Does not assess the strategic case, value for money or effectiveness of equipment and training; some information is classified.
transferable_lesson: Plan equipment replenishment and domestic training capacity alongside external military assistance to manage the effects on national readiness.
transferable_lesson_rationale: Turns the concluding need to balance support for Ukraine with UK stocks and training into a broader planning principle; no formal recommendation is issued.

seed_title: Investigation into the performance of UK Security Vetting
source_title: Investigation into the performance of UK Security Vetting
notes: Investigation excludes the effectiveness of vetting as a deterrent and the operational impact of clearance timeliness. Seed Process Evaluation label is retained separately.
evaluation_question: How is UK Security Vetting performing, what explains delays, and are recovery and modernisation efforts addressing the problems?
methods: Performance, staffing and financial-data analysis; document review; interviews with UKSV, Cabinet Office, customers and internal reviewers; and visits to York and Glasgow.
findings: Routine clearance targets were repeatedly missed as demand rose, staffing fell short and ageing IT disrupted work. Prioritising new cases and extending renewals reduced some backlogs but carried risks; transformation remained delayed.
recommendations: Agree a modernisation plan with milestones; improve governance and customer-focused performance measures; make prioritisation trade-offs explicit; and build capacity to respond to unexpected demand.
recommendation_basis: Formal recommendations, summarised
conclusions: Timely vetting remained poor despite recovery efforts. A credible transformation plan and stronger delivery arrangements were still needed to support national-security work.
note: The investigation does not assess whether vetting effectively deters or prevents malicious access to sensitive information.
transferable_lesson: Use service metrics that reflect timely, accurate outcomes for customers, and make the effects of prioritising particular cases explicit.
transferable_lesson_rationale: Recommendations 26(c) and 26(d) explicitly address customer-focused metrics, perverse incentives and prioritisation trade-offs.

seed_title: Investigation into the management of contracts by the Ministry of Defence on behalf of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia
source_title: Investigation into the management of contracts by the Ministry of Defence on behalf of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia
notes: Official webpage uses a shortened title; PDF title matches the seed. Investigation explicitly excludes value-for-money assessment because the programmes are funded by Saudi Arabia.
evaluation_question: What controls govern MoD’s Saudi-funded defence contracts, do payments comply with them, and have lessons from the earlier court case been applied?
methods: Interviews with programme and departmental officials, agreement and governance-document review, and walkthroughs and sample testing of transactions and financial controls.
findings: MODSAP and SANGCOM had clear expenditure controls and complied with them. Internal-audit actions and lessons from the court case strengthened governance, payment checks and fraud awareness.
recommendations: None issued; the investigation identified no significant areas of concern in the current arrangements examined.
recommendation_basis: No formal recommendations
conclusions: Current controls and oversight were operating as intended, with no significant concerns identified within the investigation’s scope.
note: Examines current MODSAP and SANGCOM arrangements, not historical conduct or value for money. The smaller British Military Mission was excluded.
transferable_lesson: Combine documented payment controls, transaction testing and continuing assurance when overseeing contracts for another government.
transferable_lesson_rationale: Drawn from compliant controls and strengthened assurance in the programmes examined; the investigation does not issue this as a general recommendation.

seed_title: Investigation into the Ministry of Defence's oversight of the Reserve Forces' and Cadets' Associations
source_title: Investigation into the Ministry of Defence’s oversight of the Reserve Forces’ and Cadets’ Associations
notes: Official webpage abbreviates Ministry of Defence to MoD; PDF title matches the seed. Seed Cyber domain is retained but warrants review: the report concerns reserve/cadet governance and infrastructure.
evaluation_question: Has MoD implemented the Sullivan review and established sufficient oversight of the Reserve Forces’ and Cadets’ Associations’ duties, performance and finances?
methods: Governance, legal and financial-document review; interviews with MoD and association leaders; two regional visits; and written evidence from nine further associations.
findings: Oversight had improved, but establishing a single public body required legislation and remained incomplete. Limited intervention powers, financial-reporting gaps and incomplete Treasury oversight left legal and financial risks.
recommendations: No separate formal recommendations. Concluding remarks call for mitigating remaining legal and financial risks through structural reform or stronger existing arrangements, while retaining regional connections.
recommendation_basis: No formal recommendations; actions in concluding remarks
conclusions: The associations provide important local support, but MoD needed stronger assurance that their evolving role was legally sound, financially controlled and cost-effective.
note: Does not assess associations’ operational performance, value for money or the policy choice of organisational form. The seed’s domain label is retained without endorsement.
transferable_lesson: Strengthen legal and financial oversight while retaining the benefits of regional organisations' local identities and relationships.
transferable_lesson_rationale: The concluding remarks explicitly call for mitigating legal and financial risks while retaining the associations' local benefits.

seed_title: Optimising the defence estate
source_title: Optimising the defence estate
notes: Seed Process Evaluation label is retained; publisher categorises this as a value-for-money report.
evaluation_question: Has MoD made planned progress in optimising its estate, and are its strategy and delivery arrangements sufficient to achieve value for money?
methods: Interviews, estate and financial-data analysis, review of business cases and disposal schedules, cost-model assessment and comparison with earlier audit recommendations.
findings: The built estate shrank by only 2% over five years, while forecast net benefits fell from £2.4 billion to £0.65 billion. Funding and disposal agreements improved, but delivery remained complex and cost forecasts uncertain.
recommendations: Reset realistic estate targets; review governance; address causes of disposal delays and programme dependencies; and improve data on estate requirements and full relocation/disposal costs.
recommendation_basis: Formal recommendations, summarised
conclusions: MoD was better positioned to proceed but had yet to demonstrate value for money. It needed to convert repeated replanning into completed disposals and a more affordable estate.
note: Site visits were not possible because of pandemic restrictions.
transferable_lesson: Use realistic disposal schedules and full relocation and site-preparation costs when planning estate rationalisation and forecasting its benefits.
transferable_lesson_rationale: Recommendations 22(c) and 22(d) explicitly require testing schedules and improving information on the full time and cost of disposals.

seed_title: The repurchase of the service family accommodation estate
source_title: The repurchase of the service family accommodation estate
evaluation_question: Was repurchasing service family accommodation good value for money, and has MoD established the conditions to improve future housing provision?
methods: Interviews with MoD, Treasury and UK Government Investments; review of business cases and valuation advice; discounted-cost analysis; and testing of economic-model assumptions.
findings: The £5.99 billion repurchase was well negotiated and preferable to continued leasing. However, the original sale-and-leaseback left MoD an estimated £14.5 billion worse off, and delivering better housing required capabilities and investment it still lacked.
recommendations: Secure long-term funding and expertise; establish the Defence Housing Service with suitable powers and governance; publish delivery plans; and share lessons on sale-and-leaseback risks and commercial capability.
recommendation_basis: Formal recommendations, summarised
conclusions: The repurchase offered value for money against continued leasing. Its lasting benefits depended on delivering the housing strategy and improving maintenance and management.
note: Published June 2026; assesses the December 2024 repurchase and subsequent plans. The historical loss is an estimated counterfactual comparison.
transferable_lesson: When selling and leasing back public assets, account for the long-term risks and responsibilities government retains, and use specialist commercial expertise.
transferable_lesson_rationale: Recommendations 20(e) and 20(f) explicitly identify these lessons for sharing across government.

seed_title: The Ajax programme
source_title: The Ajax programme
notes: Publication date corrected from seed 2022-03-08 to 2022-03-11, confirmed by the official webpage and PDF cover.
evaluation_question: Has the Ajax programme progressed as intended, are its delivery arrangements effective, and is MoD positioned to resolve problems and achieve value for money?
methods: Interviews, programme and contract-document review, financial and progress-data analysis, assessment of safety-trial evidence, and visits to the manufacturer and independent testing grounds.
findings: The in-service date had slipped four years, with no confirmed usable capability. Unresolved safety and technical problems, underestimated complexity and programme-management failures persisted despite £3.167 billion in contract spending.
recommendations: Agree a credible delivery schedule; strengthen governance and real-time management information; align contract incentives with capability outcomes; and ensure clear accountability for resolving safety recommendations.
recommendation_basis: Formal recommendations, summarised
conclusions: MoD had not demonstrated value for money. Delivering the intended capability required difficult decisions, resolution of safety issues and avoidance of further cost growth and delays.
note: Describes the programme at the March 2022 report date; it is not a current programme-status assessment.
transferable_lesson: Align supplier incentives with delivered capability and give safety duty holders sufficient authority to report and escalate problems.
transferable_lesson_rationale: Recommendations 22(d) and 22(e) explicitly address capability-focused incentives and the authority of safety duty holders.

seed_title: The Equipment Plan 2021 to 2031
source_title: The Equipment Plan 2021 to 2031
evaluation_question: Is the 2021–2031 Equipment Plan affordable, are its budget and cost assumptions realistic, and do planning arrangements support long-term value for money?
methods: Budget and cost-forecast analysis, business-case and savings-plan review, interviews with MoD and Treasury, and assessment of financial skills, governance and independent cost assurance.
findings: Additional funding and prioritisation eased pressures, but optimistic budget, cost and savings assumptions persisted. Inconsistent planning, financial-skills gaps and short-term balancing decisions continued to undermine affordability.
recommendations: Standardise forecasts and reporting; clarify budget responsibilities; distinguish evidenced savings from targets; review capability gaps and related spending plans; and clarify governance of submarine contingency funding.
recommendation_basis: Formal recommendations, summarised
conclusions: There remained a real risk that ambitions exceeded resources. The multi-year settlement offered an opportunity to secure affordability, but sustained reform and stronger financial management were necessary.
note: Assesses the 2021–2031 plan using evidence collected in 2021; later spending plans are separate evaluations.
transferable_lesson: Separate savings supported by delivery plans from additional savings targets when reporting long-term spending forecasts.
transferable_lesson_rationale: Recommendation 25(d) explicitly requires a distinction between cost reductions backed by clear plans and additional targets, with supporting evidence.

seed_title: The Equipment Plan 2023-2033
source_title: The Equipment Plan 2023–2033
notes: Webpage title uses 2023 to 2033; PDF cover uses 2023–2033. Both identify the same report.
evaluation_question: Is the 2023–2033 Equipment Plan affordable, how robust are its assumptions, and how is MoD responding to financial and capability pressures?
methods: Detailed budget and project-cost analysis, business-case and savings-assumption review, assessment of capability evidence and independent cost assurance, and interviews with MoD budget holders.
findings: Forecast costs exceeded the budget by £16.9 billion, the largest recorded plan deficit. Inconsistent costing obscured capability gaps, while major spending decisions were deferred until the next Spending Review.
recommendations: Assess and explain the financial and capability effects of delayed decisions; require consistent inclusion of the full predicted costs of required capabilities across budget holders.
recommendation_basis: Formal recommendations, summarised
conclusions: The plan was unaffordable and did not reliably demonstrate how equipment ambitions would be funded. Deferring decisions risked waste on programmes later cancelled, reduced or delayed.
note: The £16.9 billion gap is MoD’s central estimate at March 2023 and depends on assumptions; it is not a current deficit estimate.
transferable_lesson: Make the financial and capability consequences of postponing major spending decisions visible to decision-makers and those scrutinising them.
transferable_lesson_rationale: Recommendation 20(a) explicitly requires assessing and explaining the impact of delayed decisions to decision-makers and Parliament.

seed_title: The Ministry of Defence's management of its losses from fraud and other economic crime
source_title: The Ministry of Defence’s management of its losses from fraud and other economic crime
notes: Official webpage uses a shortened title; PDF title matches the seed. Seed Impact Evaluation label is retained; publisher categorises this as a value-for-money report.
evaluation_question: How effectively does MoD understand, investigate and reduce losses from fraud and economic crime, and where could it achieve greater savings?
methods: Analysis of hotline and police case data, sample reviews of 20 police referrals and 12 other referrals, stakeholder interviews and review of risk, governance and operating-model documents.
findings: Reported prevention and recovery were low relative to spending and likely losses. Fragmented teams, inconsistent case records, weak follow-up and poorly targeted risk analysis limited results despite recent improvements.
recommendations: Set a shared loss-reduction objective; empower senior leadership and a multidisciplinary investigation team; improve triage, risk estimates and case data; and resource preventive analytics.
recommendation_basis: Formal recommendations, summarised
conclusions: Better coordination and use of existing enforcement resources could materially reduce losses, releasing savings for defence capability.
note: Case-management datasets were incomplete and difficult to reconcile; the report does not establish the total actual loss to fraud.
transferable_lesson: Organise counter-fraud work around reducing total losses, combining prevention, disruption and recovery through shared leadership and multidisciplinary teams.
transferable_lesson_rationale: Recommendations 13(a) to 13(c) explicitly call for a shared loss-reduction objective, empowered leadership and pooled specialist resources.

seed_title: The UK's F-35 capability
source_title: The UK’s F-35 capability
evaluation_question: Is MoD delivering its intended F-35 capability and supporting requirements in a way that maximises value for money?
methods: More than 30 interviews, programme-document and financial analysis, delivery and availability-data analysis, a RAF Marham visit and an illustrative pilot/engineer focus group.
findings: F-35 improved military capability and supported UK industry, but availability, personnel, infrastructure and weapon integration lagged plans. Published cost estimates omitted substantial whole-life and supporting costs.
recommendations: Define and track military and wider benefits; report comprehensive historical and forecast costs; simplify accountability and approvals; improve leadership continuity; and measure capability against objective requirements.
recommendation_basis: Formal recommendations, summarised
conclusions: Capability delivered for an estimated £11 billion spent was disappointing against MoD plans. Better support and transparent cost and benefit measures were needed to improve value for money.
note: Reflects the July 2025 report. Some evidence was redacted for national security; the focus group was not representative.
transferable_lesson: Assess major equipment programmes using comprehensive whole-life costs and clearly weighted military and non-military benefits.
transferable_lesson_rationale: Recommendations 26(a) and 26(b) explicitly require these assessments and identify possible application to other major defence programmes.

methods: Synthesis of 16 audits/evaluations, questionnaires from 10 personnel, stakeholder consultation, document review and collaborative process mapping.
findings: Despite reforms, fragmented data, rigid requirements, heavy oversight and workforce constraints persist. Urgent procurement also faces cross-departmental barriers; new approaches require enabling conditions.

findings: Delays and optimistic schedules persist. Some rapid programmes entered with immature technologies, and adoption of iterative development practices remains inconsistent.
recommendations_or_advisory_priorities: Require rapid programmes integrating multiple technologies to start with mature technologies or develop immature elements separately.

methods: Theory of change; 606 current/lapsed-user and 516 non-user survey responses; 33 follow-up interviews, three case studies and evidence review.
findings: Users reported better risk understanding and security practices. Certification also supported supply-chain assurance; causal attribution and measurement of prevented attacks remained difficult.

source_title_as_published: Evaluation of the employer National Insurance contributions relief for veterans
date_notes: Report dated July 2023; published on GOV.UK on 28 May 2025. Fieldwork took place in early 2023.
topic_tags: Veterans; civilian employment; recruitment incentives
evaluation_question: Did employer National Insurance relief encourage veteran recruitment, and how were savings used?
methods: Nineteen qualitative interviews with claiming employers, January–February 2023, including hypothetical changes to the incentive.
findings: Interviewed employers said the relief had not driven their veteran hiring decisions. Claiming was straightforward, but savings generally supported existing expenditure or cash flow.
recommendations_or_advisory_priorities: The report questions the incentive's proportionality and appropriateness; it does not establish a population-wide employment effect.
uk_mod_relevance: Directly relevant to service-leaver employment and cooperation between MOD, employers and other government departments.
transferable_lesson: Test whether an employment incentive changes hiring decisions, rather than assuming that claims demonstrate additional jobs.
limitations: Small, non-representative claimant sample without a counterfactual group. Findings cannot establish that the relief has no effect for all employers or veterans.
priority_rationale: Strong policy relevance for veterans, but limited causal evidence and narrower MOD operational relevance.

date_notes: Published on GOV.UK on 19 September 2025; includes 2024/25 process evaluation and 2021/22–2024/25 impact/value-for-money analysis.
source_publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
topic_tags: Innovation; accelerators; cyber industry; SME growth
evaluation_question: How effectively does the accelerator support cyber businesses, and do its benefits justify its costs?
methods: Participant and unsuccessful-applicant surveys, interviews and focus groups, business and monitoring data, contribution analysis and cost-benefit modelling.
findings: Participants valued support and peer connections. Investor links and selection clarity were weaker; estimated monetised benefits exceeded costs if benefits persisted.
recommendations_or_advisory_priorities: Clarify workstreams and contact routes, provide better applicant feedback and consider more tailored support; proposed delivery changes need separate cost-effectiveness assessment.
uk_mod_relevance: Transferable evidence for defence innovation accelerators and SME support, rather than an evaluation of DASA or military capability adoption.
transferable_lesson: Assess whether accelerator benefits survive after participation and lead to customer adoption, rather than equating satisfaction with impact.
limitations: Selection, recall and response biases; unsuccessful applicants may differ systematically. Value-for-money results rely on assumptions about persistent benefits and omit some costs.
priority_rationale: Useful methodological comparator for innovation programmes, with indirect MOD applicability.
